name: Question 9
problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/multivariable/14079137/assets/b2ce73d5a44c834b5935596e85293eb92039b674746754317846488dbba8d930.png)

Calculate ${\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s,$ where $C$ is the path along the polar curve $r={e}^{\theta /4}\,$ for $0\le \theta \le 2\pi ,$ shown above.
worked_solution:
The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over $C$ is equal to the arc length $L$ of $C,$ i.e.,

$$
{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s=L.
$$

In polar coordinates, the arc length element $\text{d}s$ is given by

$$
\text{d}s=\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

So, for a polar curve defined as $r=r(\theta )$ for ${\theta }_{1}\le \theta \le {\theta }_{2},$ we have

$$
L={\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta .
$$

Since $r={e}^{\theta /4},$ we have

$$
\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta }=\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4}.
$$

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\int }_{C}\,\text{d}s & ={\int }_{{\theta }_{1}}^{{\theta }_{2}}\sqrt{{r}^{2}+{(\frac{\text{d}r}{\text{d}\theta })}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{({e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}+{(\frac{1}{4}\,{e}^{\theta /4})}^{2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{{e}^{\theta /2}+\frac{1}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{2\pi }\sqrt{\frac{17}{16}\,{e}^{\theta /2}}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\frac{\sqrt{17}}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2\pi }{e}^{\theta /4}\,\text{d}\theta  \\  & =\sqrt{17}\,{e}^{\theta /4}\,{|}_{0}^{2\pi } \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-{e}^{0}) \\  & =\sqrt{17}({e}^{\pi /2}-1).\end{aligned}
$$

Question 9
?

Calculate ∫Cds, where C is the path along the polar curve r=eθ/4 for 0≤θ≤2π, shown above.

a
13(eπ/4−1)
b
5(eπ/4−1)
c
17(eπ/2−1)
d
10(eπ/2−1)
e
4(eπ/2−1)
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

The line integral of unity with respect to arc length over C is equal to the arc length L of C, i.e., ∫Cds=L.

In polar coordinates, the arc length element ds is given by ds=r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

So, for a polar curve defined as r=r(θ) for θ1≤θ≤θ2, we have L=∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ.

Since r=eθ/4, we have drdθ=14eθ/4.

Therefore, we evaluate our line integral as follows: ∫Cds=∫θ1θ2r2+(drdθ)2dθ=∫02π(eθ/4)2+(14eθ/4)2dθ=∫02πeθ/2+116eθ/2dθ=∫02π1716eθ/2dθ=174∫02πeθ/4dθ=17eθ/4|02π=17(eπ/2−e0)=17(eπ/2−1).
